I'm curious if there is a comprehensive and concise document of the type theory that is modeled versus the one Lean implements, with all gaps explained very clearly. I did something like this with my students in the course I taught last semester for the proof assistant we built, for example: https://github.com/nicegeo/nicegeo/blob/main/METATHEORY.md

Even though for us, a verified kernel was wildly out of scope, I made sure we had this because the most consequential bugs often manifest in these gaps

The approach lean4lean takes is a bit simpler than my masters thesis: There is one typing relation, the "idealized" one, which satisfies transitivity and subject reduction and is not decidable. Then there is a kernel program, which is sound but not complete (or at least it should be, and most soundness bugs are in this part). So recast in these terms, the question is: where is the lean checker not complete?

There are a few known places:

  • The checking of unit-like types is not complete. It checks only Unit (and similar inductives) and propositions, but it should also include pi types whose codomain is unit-like and structures containing only unit-like types.
  • The level algorithm is incomplete. Lean4lean has a potential replacement algorithm that should be complete.
  • Lean does not compute through some large eliminating subsingleton inductives, including Acc and Quot. For Acc in particular this would cause lean to not terminate when typechecking some things, so it is understandable that lean doesn't do this, but it could at least be gated in a more principled way, e.g. by having a fuel amount controlling unfolding.

This is all I can recall; it's plausible that if you fix those then you can prove a completeness theorem for typechecking.
How are nested inductives handled?
badly :)

it still remains to determine how to even specify what a nested inductive is supposed to be, and until that work is done we can't prove either soundness or completeness. @Arthur Adjedj has expressed some interest in working on the nested inductive spec

I would argue that extending a "naive" strict positivity criteria for non-nested types to handle nesteds will not be absurdly hard. In particular, a formal specification of Rocq’s nested positivity criteria already exists, and Lean’s resembles it closely (I can take the time to explicit the differences if someone is interested in looking into this). I plan on working on either a specification for base inductive types or for nesteds based on existing Rocq work in a month or so, depending of the state of things by that time.
Is there a model where strict positivity is intrinsic? Something like https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08837

Kovacs’ work on theories of signatures is, to my knowledge, the most "intrinsic" presentation of inductive types around. Lean4Lean relies on extrinsic properties anyway, so the inductive formalisms will surely do so too

So I think when I talk about the gap, I want to capture this sort of thing. How does that fall into the discussion above?

Also, I assume you are aware of the POPL paper I linked to in the other thread on justifiable nested inductives in Rocq and Lean?

i.e., https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3808322

In addition to documenting current gaps, I'd super recommend talking to these folks if you haven't already. Happy to open up that conversation and connect folks if needed
Yes, I had a conversation with Thomas Lamiaux a few days ago about how to do nested inductives, it will need some adaptation but both me and Arthur are aware of it

Cool. Curious how to classify those kinds of gaps and document them. Happy to help with some documentation and related work for that (I have strep though so may take some time) if you know where those kinds of features fall

if you talk to @Meven Lennon-Bertrand he'll argue for having a proof also of "negative soundness", i.e. if the typechecker says a typing or defeq doesn't hold then it doesn't, even if there is an in between possibility for nontermination. Currently I make no attempt to prove negative provability facts, but that's basically how you would establish completeness
Meven's paper What Does It Take to Certify a Conversion Checker? talks about what you need to do to certify negative soundness properties

By the way, I think this is what people call partial correctness, and I think it is a clearer name than negative soundness.

It does make sense to me that the Rocq and Lean folks should collaborate here since some of the lesser understood type theoretic features are common to both, though attention to the divergence also needs to be paid because of the existence of fire triangles etc

That you don't need to handle coinductives, and that you have primitive eliminators, definitely makes your job easier along a few dimensions than in Rocq, though definitional equality is weirder in Lean.
IIRC there are some primitive projections in Lean? How are those handled
well, tell that to the people that want to add primitive coinductives to lean :upside_down:
omg haha
there are indeed primitive projections. They are handled as if they were abbreviations for recursor expressions
although you can't actually do that desugaring without typechecking so it's not entirely trivial

I ask about primitive projections in particular because, back in 2016 or so when I was in France, Pierre-Marie told me he strongly suspected that Rocq's nested inductives were unsound in combination with primitive projections (which are an optional thing in Rocq disabled by default)
That is based on hazy memory, but I'd loop Pierre-Marie into the nested inductives conversation too
If you can handle the snark that is inherent to his personality and is never personal lol

the soundness bug list Michael Rothgang just posted indeed contains a few related to primitive projections, but I don't think there is a specific reason to be worried about them wrt nested inductives because nested inductives don't have structure eta
actually maybe they do when nesting through a structure :thinking:
fun times

If folks do add coinductive types, I think my students Trey Plante and @Eric Paul understand them very well after some of our recent type theory & proof repair work, but mostly my takeaway is that nobody does them correctly at all right now except Cubical Agda....

My hope is that our last POPL paper clears the last major hurdle, but that's not really true; there is still work to determine how to make it handle constants in general and rewrites, and two recent Gallinette papers Definitional Proof Irrelevance Made Accessible and Consolidating Equality in a Proof Irrelevant Universe are just what we need, so we "just" need to incorporate the tricks from those papers into our paper into lean4lean

I also highly suspect more features will continue to be added to Lean's kernel over time, since this happens in every proof assistant, so having something regular on that end might help in the future too

A quick command I did seems to indicate nested types are used in a fair amount of places:

import Lean
import Mathlib

open Lean Elab Meta Command

run_cmd liftTermElabM do
  let env ← getEnv
  let mut nestedTypes : List Name := []
  for (declName,_) in env.constants do
    try
      let indVal ← getConstInfoInduct declName
      if indVal.numNested != 0 then
        nestedTypes := declName::nestedTypes
    catch _ => continue
  logInfo m!"number of nested types {nestedTypes.length} : \n {nestedTypes}"

The main point of nested inductive types is that they allow for modularly reusing existing APIs. In theory, you could replace any nested inductive type to a mutual inductive type, similarly to what the kernel does internally, but that would imply having to duplicate any API around the type you nested under for the use-case of this new one, leading to a lot of duplicated code and complications. Lean 3 used to not have nested types at the type theory level, and the need for those seems to have manifested clearly enough for them to become part of the kernel when transitioning to Lean 4. I don't think getting rid of them would be a step in the right direction.
I can think of two related uses : unbounded fan-in circuits (see my library), and, well, trees.

I was considering proposing that checkers could track which feature are used by a development, and maybe AI based math projects would just have a policy of not using nested inductives. Many of the ones listed by Arthur are in meta code and would not show up in the exported slice of a main theorem. But maybe this direction is more confusing than helpful to users.

I already avoid nested inductives in all languages whenever tractable. But they show up a lot with programming language and compiler verification and metatheory, and rose trees etc. Ideally, they should not add any expressive power over vanilla inductives, but the transformation is wildly nontrivial to do manually and as actually implemented, that statement isn't even true anyways

I think in an ideal world it might be that they are implemented as sugar that elaborate to vanilla inductives (with mutual inductives as a step in between), much like primitive pattern matching is a mistake and Lean did that right. But this would be a major change to the scope of types supported, based on extremely recent type theory results, using transformations that would be wildly nontrivial to implement
But in the world we live in I think we just need to reimplement nested inductives to be the intended fragment to begin with based on those recent results
